title: Errors in a client portal
metaTitle: When a promised file will not open
excerpt: When a promised file fails to open, say what broke and how to get it. A code and a sad illustration waste a client who needed the file for their own meeting.
alt: An open notebook with the word Notes underlined, a fountain pen, and glasses on a wooden desk, a page that still has to say what went wrong.
caption: The note should say what failed, in words a client can use. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a portal say when a file will not open?
faqs.answer: Name the file and say whether a download is still possible, then offer one next step, usually try again or download, and leave them signed in. A code and a sad illustration waste a client who is trying to get the file into their own meeting. If the preview failed and the file is fine, say that the preview failed.

faqs.question: What if the link expired?
faqs.answer: Say the link expired and whether a fresh sign-in will still reach the file. Send them to sign in if that is the remedy, and land them on the file afterward, not on a generic home. If the link is dead because the file was replaced, name the current file. Do not show a bare error page with no project name.

faqs.question: Should the client see a server error code?
faqs.answer: Put a code only as small type under a sentence that names the file and the next step. The code is for the studio if they have to write for help. Leading with the code tells the client the failure is theirs to decode.

markdown:
Client portal error states are the sentences a client reads when the file they were promised will not open. Say what broke and what to do. They may be minutes from their own meeting. A code and a sad illustration waste that moment and make the studio look careless with the work.

Keep them in the portal. Keep the project name on screen. Tell them whether the file is still there. If you dump them at a blank error with no way back, they will email someone in a panic, and the file was probably fine.

## Name the file that failed

Say the file's human title. The logo pack did not open. The homepage document did not download. "Something went wrong" is how you turn a preview bug into a lost deliverable in their mind.

Say which half failed. The preview failed and the download is available. The download failed and they should retry. The file was replaced and here is the current one. Those are three different recoveries. One illustration of a broken folder covers none of them.

Then one action. Try the download. Open the current file. Sign in again. The action should be a real button, in the same view as the file's name. A link that says "click here" at the end of a paragraph is easy to miss when they are annoyed.

Use the noun from the email. If you promised brand files, the error says brand files. "Asset id 441 could not be fetched" is the storage layer talking. The client has an asset only if you taught them that word. You should not have taught them that word.

The W3C's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines exist so a message is perceivable, operable, and understandable. A portal error that is only a picture, or only a red banner with no text, fails a client who is stressed and may be using a screen reader on the way into a room. [The WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the standard to put next to the template. Words first. A reference code last, in small type, for the studio.

## The failures worth writing down

You do not need a unique drawing for each. You need a sentence in the design file before the first client link goes out.

Preview failed. Common for large files and for types the browser cannot render. Say the preview failed. Offer the download in the same breath. Do not imply the file is corrupt when only the thumbnail is.

Download failed. The network dropped or the file is temporarily unavailable. Say whether they should retry now. Leave the page in the project. A retry that starts over at the marketing site is a second failure.

Link expired. Say that, and say that the project is still there if they sign in. After sign-in, open the file the link pointed at, not a dashboard. If the file is gone, say it was removed or replaced, and name the replacement if there is one.

Wrong account. They are signed into a different email. Say which email is signed in, without exposing another client's data, and offer a switch. "You are signed in as ada@client.com. This link is for a different account." That sentence prevents a terrifying empty project that looks like you deleted their work.

Upload failed, if clients upload too. Their version did not replace the studio's file. Say so, so they do not present a file the studio never received. Keep their selected file named on screen so they can retry without hunting through a desktop.

Permission denied is adjacent and easy to mislabel as a crash. If they are not allowed to download, that is a rule, and the next article treats it as one. In the error, do not say "failed" if you mean "not shared." Failed sounds temporary. Not shared is a decision. Mixing them creates a support thread about a bug that is actually a setting.

The list to put beside the happy path:

- Preview failed, download offered
- Download failed, retry in place
- Link expired, sign in returns to the file
- Wrong account, the signed-in email shown
- Upload did not land, their filename kept
- Not shared, said as a rule, not as a crash

If one cannot happen, mark it so the template does not grow a mascot later.

## Keep the project on screen

The client should still see the project name and the file name while the error is up. Those are the landmarks from the email. A full-screen illustration deletes the landmarks and leaves a mood. Mood is not a way back.

Do not sign them out because one file failed. Sign-out feels like punishment and loses their place. Repair in the session. If the session is the problem, say the session expired and send them through sign-in back to this file.

Toasts are too weak for this. They vanish, and the client is left wondering if the download started. An inline message on the file row stays. If the failure is the whole page, the page itself is the message, with the project name in the header and one button.

A joke about missing files, coffee spills, or robots is the wrong tone. They may be about to show this work to their own customer. Plain speech respects that. The logo pack did not open. You can download it instead.

Give the studio a code they can use, under the sentence, and also write the human sentence into your own log. When the client writes "it broke," you want the log to say which sentence they saw. Otherwise you will debug the wrong half.

## Do not make them rebuild the path

"Go to dashboard" is a poor recovery. The dashboard is where people get lost on a good day. The recovery is the file, the download, or the current version.

If the file was replaced, link the replacement in the error. "This pack was replaced on Tuesday. Open the current logo pack." Make that button the primary one. Leave the old file available only if you mean them to have it. Two packs with equal weight, one of them retired, is how the wrong marks get presented.

If nothing can be done in the product, say what happens next in one line. "We can see this failure." Only say that if it is true. A lie about automatic notification is worse than a quiet line that tells them to reply to the person who sent the file. Do not invent a help desk you do not have. A named person they already know is the honest path.

Keep the visual calm. This screen does not need a new color system. It needs contrast that still works if they are outside, and type large enough to read while walking into a building. The filename is the largest text after the explanation.


## The email and the portal have to agree

Clients will try the attachment and the portal. If the email still carries an older file and the portal holds the current one, say that in the portal and stop attaching the old one. An error that says the portal file failed, while the email file opens, teaches them to ignore the portal. That undoes the handoff. One source of the current file is enough, and the error copy should point at it.

If there is no attachment on purpose, the email should say the file lives in the portal, and a failed link should still name the file they expected. Mentioning the day of the email helps them find the thread in their inbox, and it is not a substitute for the retry button. Context plus a retry is the repair. Context alone is a shrug.

Copy the human sentence into the note you keep when a download fails. You want to see that the logo pack preview failed, not only a status code. When they reply to the original thread, your answer can match the screen they are looking at. Two descriptions of one failure, theirs and the log's, waste the hour before their meeting. The log can keep the code. It should also keep the sentence.
## Review it the way a client panics

Open a real file link in a browser that cannot preview that type. You should see the filename and a download. Expire a link and confirm sign-in returns to the file. Sign in as the wrong test client and confirm you do not see the other client's titles in the error. Leaking a name in an error string is a serious bug wearing a friendly template.

Throttle the network and start a download. The page should say the download did not finish, and it should let them retry without finding the email again.

Then separate rules from crashes. The next piece is [permissions in a client portal](/blog/permissions-in-a-client-portal). A file that is view-only, or not shared yet, should say so before it looks broken. Clients report both as "the portal is down."

If those sentences should be designed with the portal, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). The file is the work. The error is part of handing it over. A mascot is not a handoff.
